meta.title: Who really said "The die is cast"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Julius Caesar said it at the Rubicon in 49 BC — but the famous English wording follows Suetonius's Latin, while Plutarch says Caesar spoke Greek: "let the die be cast."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The die is cast'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Caesar — at the Rubicon in 49 BC. But the exact wording comes from Suetonius's Latin; Plutarch records a Greek imperative, "let the die be cast."

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Caesar reportedly said this at the crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BC. Suetonius records the Latin iacta alea est ↗, conventionally Englished as “the die is cast.” But Plutarch says Caesar spoke in Greek ↗ — an imperative, “let the die be cast” — so the familiar wording follows Suetonius’s translation rather than Caesar’s own words.

source.heading: The saying at the Rubicon

docMeta.dd: iacta alea est (“the die has been cast”)

source.excerpt: Then Caesar cried, “Take we the course which the signs of the gods and the false dealing of our foes point out. The die is cast,” said he.
trail: Suetonius reports the Latin iacta alea est, while Plutarch and Appian give the Greek anerrhíphthω kýbos, “let the die be cast” ↗.
Wiktionary calls the English idiom a calque of Suetonius’s Latin — and a “grammatically incorrect” rendering of the Greek ↗.
The Greek line is thought to quote a comedy by Menander; both historians wrote long after Caesar’s death ↗.
source.excerptNote: Suetonius, Divus Iulius 32, in the English of J. C. Rolfe’s public-domain Loeb translation. Plutarch (Caesar 32) and Appian instead report the Greek ἀνερρίφθω κύβος — an imperative, “let the die be cast.”
source.rightsNote: The Latin and Greek originals are ancient and long in the public domain, and the English idiom “the die is cast” predates 1931 by centuries — it appears in early-modern translations of Suetonius and the public-domain 1913 Loeb rendering by J. C. Rolfe. No modern rights attach to this three-word phrase.

author.name: Julius Caesar
author.heading: Who was Julius Caesar?
author.bio: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BC ignited the civil war that ended the Roman Republic. Fluent in Greek and a noted stylist, he was famously terse — the tradition that he marked the moment with a gambler’s tag fits both the man and his admiration for the playwright Menander.

copyAttribution: The die is cast — attributed to Julius Caesar at the crossing of the Rubicon, 49 BC, as recorded in Latin by Suetonius (Life of the Deified Julius 32: "iacta alea est"). Plutarch reports Caesar spoke Greek, in the imperative: "let the die be cast."

misattribution.heading: Right man, contested words
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t pinned on the wrong person — Caesar really is the speaker. What’s off is the wording: the famous English line comes from Suetonius’s Latin, not from Caesar’s mouth.

items.why: The English “the die is cast” translates Suetonius’s Latin indicative iacta alea est. Plutarch says Caesar actually spoke Greek and used an imperative — “let the die be cast” ↗ — a call to venture, not a statement of inevitability.
The Greek phrase Caesar exclaimed is widely held to quote a comedy by the Athenian playwright Menander ↗, already a well-known tag among educated Romans.

misattribution.truthLine: Caesar said something at the Rubicon in 49 BC; the English “the die is cast” is a calque of Suetonius’s Latin, which itself imperfectly renders the Greek imperative ↗ that Plutarch preserved.

context.heading: A point of no return
lead: To cross the Rubicon — the river marking the boundary of Caesar’s province — with his army was to defy the Senate and start a civil war. The saying has since become shorthand for any irrevocable decision.

The two ancient versions carry different feeling. Suetonius’s Latin states a fact: the throw has happened, there is no going back. Plutarch’s Greek is an exhortation: let the die be thrown — a gambler’s dare to fortune.
context.pull: The die is cast — or, in the Greek Plutarch heard, “let the die be cast.”
